n: Chapter 1 mourns the destruction and desolation of Jerusalem, recognizing that this was God’s well-deserved judgment on Israel’s sins.

Chapters 1 and 2 are alphabet poems.

Chapter 1 compared Jerusalem to a woman who weeps. The city was described as a widow whose children had been killed. This described how the people of Jerusalem felt when Babylon attacked them.

Babylonian armies surrounded Jerusalem for many months. The people in Jerusalem didn’t have enough food and they couldn’t get more. They suffered terribly. People were so hungry that they ate the bodies of their children who had died.

In 587 and 586 BC the Babylonians entered the city. They killed many people and forced many others to live in Babylon. They also destroyed the temple. These terrible events were part of the covenant curses.

In the first poem, the people of Jerusalem recognised why they were suffering. It was because they had refused to obey God. God had finally brought judgement against them for the evil things they had done.

Chapter 2 described this judgement as the cloud of God’s anger. In these chapters the speakers recognised that God was right to bring judgement. At the same time, the speakers urged the people to pray to God for mercy.

The speakers also complained against God. They accused him of being their enemy. They accused God of killing his people (God’s people) without pity. It was hard for the people of Jerusalem to accept what had happened to them.

The speakers were honest with God about how they felt. They asked God many questions. They told God how much they had been crying. They complained to God about things that were hard. They protested about things that seemed to be unfair. They asked God to punish their enemies. In these ways the poems were like many poems in the book of Psalms.

The lovers were the fertility gods, Baal and Asherah, whom most people in Judah worshiped. who were worshiped by most people in Judah. Her friends were her military allies, notably Egypt, who was not strong enough to defeat Babylon in battle ({{Jeremiah 37:5-11|Jeremiah 37:5–11}}).

- The woman in {{Lamentations 1:1|Lamentations 1:1}} represents the nation of Judah. The writer describes Judah as a woman who now sits alone and suffers.

- *gone into exile*: The people of Judah were led away into captivity (forced to leave their land and live in another country). This happened four times: 

- In 605 BC, some young men were taken to Babylon ({{Daniel 1:3-4|Daniel 1:3–4}}).

- In 597 BC, King Jehoiachin and many others were taken away ({{2 Kings 24:12-16|2 Kings 24:12–16}}; {{Jeremiah 52:28|Jeremiah 52:28}}; {{Ezekiel 1:2-3|Ezekiel 1:2–3}}).

- In 586 BC, Jerusalem was destroyed and more people were taken into exile ({{2 Kings 25:5-7|2 Kings 25:5–7}}, {{2 Kings 25:18-21|18–21}}; {{Jeremiah 39:5-10|Jeremiah 39:5–10}}; {{Jeremiah 52:29|52:29}}).

- In 581 BC, another group was taken away after the fall of Jerusalem ({{Jeremiah 52:30|Jeremiah 52:30}}).

- *Zion*: In the Psalms and prophetic books, Zion represents the city of Jerusalem. In Lamentations, Zion is a poetic name for the city of Jerusalem. The writer uses this name even when the city lies in ruins (destroyed buildings and broken walls). {{Hebrews 12:22-24|Hebrews 12:22–24}} speaks of the heavenly Zion (see also {{Revelation 14:1-5|Revelation 14:1–5}}). 

- The annual festivals in Jerusalem included: 

- The Passover

- The Feast of Unleavened Bread

- The Feast of the Firstfruits (also called the Feast of First Harvest)

- The Feast of Harvest (also called Pentecost)

- The Feast of Trumpets

- The Day of Atonement

- The Feast of Tabernacles (also called the Feast of Shelters)

These festivals reminded the people of what God had done for them and helped them renew their covenant (promises between God and his people). 

- The priests mainly worked in the temple and its surrounding area. When the temple was in ruins, they had no jobs and no future.

*because of her many transgression*: Judah's sins before the Babylonian invasion are described in {{2 Kings 21:1-9|2 Kings 21:1–9}}, {{2 Kings 21:16|16}}; {{2 Kings 24:3-4|24:3–4}} (compare {{2 Chronicles 33:1-10|2 Chronicles 33:1–10}}, {{2 Chronicles 33:22-23|22–23}} and {{2 Chronicles 36:11-16|2 Chronicles 36:11–16}}). Similarly, a list of Israel's sins before Assyria destroyed it is found in {{2 Kings 17:14-23|2 Kings 17:14–23}}.
Jerusalem lost everything the people valued, both physical things and spiritual blessings.
For historical accounts of these events, see {{2 Kings 25:8-17|2 Kings 25:8–17}}; {{2 Chronicles 36:13-21|2 Chronicles 36:13–21}}; {{Jeremiah 52:4-30|Jeremiah 52:4–30}}.
The destruction of Jerusalem by the Babylonians was sudden and overwhelming, like a fire sent from heaven (that is, destruction believed to come from God).

Because of their sins, the people of Judah were punished. The Babylonians tied them together with ropes and took them away as captives (prisoners of war). They forced them to go into exile (to live in a foreign land).

- *the Virgin Daughter of Judah*: God cared for Jerusalem, like a father protecting his daughter. But she continued to sin, and her punishment was horrible.

- *Like grapes in a winepress*: In ancient times, people crushed grapes by walking on them in a winepress (a large container used to press out juice). The juice flowed out as the grapes were crushed. This image shows how complete and forceful the punishment was.

Isaiah uses this picture to describe judgment in {{Isaiah 63:3|Isaiah 63:3}}. In {{Revelation 14:18-20|Revelation 14:18–20}} and {{Revelation 19:15|19:15}}, this image describes God’s judgment on the whole earth.

- *I called out to my lovers*: Egypt was very interested in Judah because Judah controlled the only good route to the north. However, Egypt abandoned Judah when Babylon attacked Jerusalem ({{Jeremiah 37:5-11|Jeremiah 37:5–11}}). 

- When there was little rain in the fall and spring in Palestine, a summer without rain could ruin crops and cause a food shortage. The food supply also ran out during the long siege of a city, which lasted from January 588 to July 586 BC. Many people starved to death ({{2 Kings 25:2-3|2 Kings 25:2–3}}; compare {{Jeremiah 37:21|Jeremiah 37:21}}).

The leaders and people of Judah had rebelled ({{Jeremiah 2:17|Jeremiah 2:17}}; {{Jeremiah 5:6|5:6}}, {{Jeremiah 5:23|23}}) by rejecting the one true God and his commandments. They also resisted the invaders God had sent ({{2 Kings 24:1|2 Kings 24:1}}, {{2 Kings 24:20|20}}; {{2 Chronicles 36:13|2 Chronicles 36:13}}).

*the day You have announced*: The poet felt encouraged by the belief that God would establish a day for fair judgment of both oppressors and victims (see {{Isaiah 13:6|Isaiah 13:6}}, {{Isaiah 13:9|9}}; {{Jeremiah 46:10-12|Jeremiah 46:10–12}}, {{Jeremiah 46:27-28|27–28}}; {{Amos 5:18-20|Amos 5:18–20}}; {{Obadiah 15|Obadiah 1:15}}; {{1 Thessalonians 5:2-3|1 Thessalonians 5:2–3}}; {{2 Thessalonians 2:2|2 Thessalonians 2:2}}).

- *heaven*: Jerusalem’s buildings were beautiful and impressive. Some were covered with precious metals and decorated with jewels. The city was known as the sacred city of the Lord.

- *his footstool*: Compare {{1 Chronicles 28:2|1 Chronicles 28:2}}; {{Psalm 99:5|Psalms 99:5}}; {{Psalm 132:7|132:7}}.
This chapter vividly shows the Lord acting as the one who destroys Jerusalem.

*bent His bow*: In the past, the Lord had been a powerful warrior for Israel (see {{Exodus 14:13-15:21|Exodus 14:13–15:21}}; {{Joshua 23:9-11|Joshua 23:9–11}}; {{Judges 7:1-25|Judges 7}}; {{2 Kings 19:32-35|2 Kings 19:32–35}}). Now he waged war against Jerusalem (see {{Isaiah 63:10|Isaiah 63:10}}; {{Ezekiel 24:25|Ezekiel 24:25}}).

A garden shelter was a temporary structure that harvesters set up to provide shade. God had promised to care for his temple forever ({{1 Kings 9:3|1 Kings 9:3}}), but now it seemed he had abandoned it.

The temple was destroyed because the priests and the people sinned inside it. Their sins made the temple ceremonially unclean and brought God’s judgment on it (see {{Jeremiah 7:3-15|Jeremiah 7:3–15}}; {{Jeremiah 26:3-6|26:3–6}}, {{Jeremiah 26:12-13|12–13}}; {{Ezekiel 24:21|Ezekiel 24:21}}).
Ramparts were stone walls or earth mounds built around a city to protect it from enemy attacks.

*no vision*: Daniel and Ezekiel were prophets of the Lord. They had visions while living among the exiles far from Judah ({{Ezekiel 1:1|Ezekiel 1:1}}; {{Daniel 7:1|Daniel 7:1}}). This verse, however, speaks about prophets in Jerusalem. These prophets claimed to receive visions from God, but their visions were false.

- Burlap, also known as *sackcloth*, was made from goat or camel hair. People often used it for grain sacks or to carry items on pack animals. Poor people wore it as clothing because it was cheap. People in mourning wore it to show their deep sorrow. Its dark color matched their mood, and its roughness matched their discomfort. 

- Throwing dust on their heads and clothing signaled to neighbors that a family member had died.

*Who can ever heal you?*: There was no one left who could bring healing. The prophets and healers who were trusted by the people had spoken lies and given false hope ({{Jeremiah 6:13-14|Jeremiah 6:13–14}}).
Their enemies were glad that Jerusalem was defeated.

*His decree, which He ordained in days of old*: God's promises of blessings depended on Israel's obedience to the law ({{Deuteronomy 8:1-20|Deuteronomy 8}}). He had promised to destroy them if they disobeyed it ({{Leviticus 26:1-46|Leviticus 26}}).
Repentance and prayer are the proper responses when facing the devastation of God’s judgment.

Jeremiah had warned that the same cannibalism (people eating human flesh during extreme hunger) that happened during the siege of Samaria ({{2 Kings 6:28-29|2 Kings 6:28–29}}) would also happen in Jerusalem ({{Jeremiah 19:9|Jeremiah 19:9}}; see also {{Lamentations 4:10|Lamentations 4:10}}; {{Ezekiel 5:10|Ezekiel 5:10}}; compare {{Deuteronomy 28:53-57|Deuteronomy 28:53–57}}).

*summoned … for the day of an appointed feast*: The poet compares Jerusalem's destruction to a feast where war, famine, wild animals, and sickness consume the wicked in Jerusalem ({{Deuteronomy 28:15-68|Deuteronomy 28:15–68}}; compare {{Revelation 19:17-21|Revelation 19:17–21}}).
The author speaks of the suffering of Judah and Jerusalem as his own.

In this chapter, the author mourns what has happened ({{Lamentations 3:1-20|Lamentations 3:1–20}}, {{Lamentations 3:48-54|48–54}}). In this chapter, the author mourns what has happened ({{Lamentations 3:21-25|Lamentations 3:21–25}}). He explains how God’s people should respond ({{Lamentations 3:26-47|Lamentations 3:26–47}}). Finally, he calls out to the Lord in prayer ({{Lamentations 3:55-66|Lamentations 3:55–66}}).

Chapters 3 and 4 are also alphabet poems. They continue talking about the terrible things that had happened in Jerusalem. They continue talking about the pain and anger of the people of the southern kingdom.

Yet there are words of hope in the middle of chapter 3. This is the centre of the book. God didn’t completely destroy his people. This was a sign that he was still committed to them. God had promised to forgive his people if they repented and turned away from their sin. He had promised this in the Mount Sinai covenant. So the speaker invited God’s people to pray to God and return to him. They could do this because they trusted that God is good. They trusted that he loved them. They believed that God was concerned about them and was faithful to them.

After these words of hope, the poems continue talking about sad things. The people were suffering as a result of their sin. In this way their suffering was different from Job’s suffering. But the people described God in ways that Job described him. Like Job, they described God as a lion waiting to attack them. They felt like God was shooting arrows at them. These were pictures that showed how confused the people felt. God’s people were completely shocked by God. It seemed that God had turned against them. They understood that they had sinned. But they couldn’t understand why God allowed them to suffer so terribly.

The way that chapter 5 is written shows how confused they felt. This poem doesn’t follow the order of the alphabet like the other poems in Lamentations do. At the end of chapter 5 the people recognised something important. They needed God to take action to help them. They needed him to bring them back to him. Only then could they return to him like chapter 3 talked about. Yet the people didn’t feel any hope or trust. They wondered if God’s anger was so complete that he had deserted them for ever.
Some interpreters understand these verses as a poetic description of Jeremiah’s time in a muddy cistern (a deep water pit) before the destruction of Jerusalem ({{Jeremiah 38:6-13|Jeremiah 38:6–13}}).

*barred my ways … made my paths crooked*: This image describes confusion and trouble. Sin can block a person’s path and make life difficult. It can prevent a person or a community from experiencing a hopeful future.

In the Bible, a straight road often represents a good and clear future. Proverbs says that innocent people walk on a straight path ({{Proverbs 21:8|Proverbs 21:8}}). Isaiah describes the Lord coming on a straight road that his worshipers would prepare ({{Isaiah 40:3|Isaiah 40:3}}).

*is wormwood and the gall*: Wormwood is a plant with a bitter taste. Here, it represents deep emotional pain ({{Proverbs 5:4|Proverbs 5:4}}; {{Revelation 8:11|Revelation 8:11}}). 

Gall refers to a poisonous plant. If someone eats it, it causes strong physical pain. Because of this, it became a symbol for extreme suffering and distress ({{Deuteronomy 29:18|Deuteronomy 29:18}}; {{Psalm 69:21|Psalm 69:21}}). 

The author feels trapped, as if there is no way out of his suffering.

The faithful love of the Lord is the reason the poet begins to recover from deep despair (great sadness). The Lord’s love gives him hope again.

This experience is like Jeremiah’s rescue from a muddy cistern ({{Jeremiah 38:6-13|Jeremiah 38:6–13}}) and Jonah’s rescue from the belly of the great fish ({{Jonah 2:2-10|Jonah 2:2–10}}). In each case, the Lord saved his servant from death.
God's love and faithfulness never end. Just as God was faithful in judging Jerusalem for their sins, he will be faithful in restoring those who return to him.

God’s faithfulness means that he is completely reliable. We see this in his daily mercies, which are new each day.

He continues to provide a world in which people can live safely.

*The LORD is my portion*: The land of Canaan was seen as Israel’s inheritance since the time of Moses ({{Exodus 15:17|Exodus 15:17}}; {{Joshua 21:19|Joshua 21:19}}; {{1 Chronicles 28:8|1 Chronicles 28:8}}; {{Psalm 47:4|Psalm 47:4}}). However, the true inheritance for God's people is God himself (see {{Psalm 16:5-6|Psalm 16:5–6}}; {{Ephesians 1:11|Ephesians 1:11}}; {{Hebrews 9:15|Hebrews 9:15}}; {{1 Peter 1:3-4|1 Peter 1:3–4}}).
Those who trust in God’s plan can wait patiently and quietly for him to bring deliverance (rescue and restoration).
*sit alone in silence*: Humble submission keeps you from speaking and calms your heart.

- In the ancient Near East, lying face down in the dust showed submission ({{Genesis 17:1-3|Genesis 17:1–3}}; {{Leviticus 9:24|Leviticus 9:24}}; {{Joshua 7:6|Joshua 7:6}}; {{1 Samuel 5:4|1 Samuel 5:4}}; {{1 Kings 18:39|1 Kings 18:39}}; {{1 Chronicles 21:16|1 Chronicles 21:16}}; {{Matthew 17:5-6|Matthew 17:5–6}}). 

- To turn the other cheek shows a willingness to submit rather than fight back. Jesus likely had this verse in mind when he taught his disciples to accept persecution ({{Matthew 5:39|Matthew 5:39}}). 

This response shows trust that God rules over all things, even over suffering.

The people of Judah were doing such things before Jerusalem was destroyed (see {{Jeremiah 5:26-31|Jeremiah 5:26–31}}; {{Jeremiah 21:11-14|21:11–14}}; {{Jeremiah 23:10-14|23:10–14}}; {{Micah 3:1-12|Micah 3}}).

Some disasters have natural causes ({{Luke 13:1-5|Luke 13:1–5}}). Bad things happen to both good and bad people ({{Matthew 5:45|Matthew 5:45}}). No matter what happens, we should give thanks and not complain ({{1 Thessalonians 5:18|1 Thessalonians 5:18}}).
Repentance is essential for receiving salvation ({{Isaiah 1:27|Isaiah 1:27}}; {{Jeremiah 3:22|Jeremiah 3:22}}; {{Ezekiel 3:21|Ezekiel 3:21}}).
The author emphasizes how cruel the enemies are and cries out to the Lord for help.
This passage might refer to Jeremiah’s experience in the cistern ({{Jeremiah 37:11-15|Jeremiah 37:11–15}}; {{Jeremiah 38:1-13|38:1–13}}).
Jerusalem deserved punishment, but the enemies carried it out with undeserved cruelty. The writer calls upon God to punish them.
This prayer for vengeance is similar to several psalms (see “Prayers for Vengeance” Theme Note).
Although God’s people still experience his judgment, they will soon experience restoration.
*their appearance like sapphires*: (literally *like lapis lazuli*): Lapis lazuli is a beautiful blue stone. It is soft enough to carve and is often used in decorations and mosaics.
Skin sticking to bones is symptomatic of the final stages of starvation, just before death.
Long sieges result in a serious lack of food. Even if people could get to the fields, they would find the crops destroyed or harvested to feed the soldiers.

*The kings of the earth … could enter the gates of Jerusalem*: Since God had saved Jerusalem from Sennacherib of Assyria over a century earlier ({{2 Kings 19:36-37|2 Kings 19:36–37}}), the Judeans firmly believed that even the powerful king Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon could not conquer the city.
It appears that these leaders fled from Jerusalem as refugees to other lands.

*The LORD’s anointed … was captured*: This refers to King Zedekiah. He tried to escape from Jerusalem, but the Babylonian army captured him. King Nebuchadnezzar treated him cruelly after his capture ({{2 Kings 25:4-7|2 Kings 25:4–7}}; {{Jeremiah 39:4-7|Jeremiah 39:4–7}}; {{Jeremiah 52:9-11|52:9–11}}).
Uz was a region east of the Jordan River. It extended south to Edom. Uz was the homeland of Job ({{Job 1:1|Job 1:1}}).

The people of Edom felt safe and took pleasure in Jerusalem's troubles. However, they would also face punishment for their sins (see {{Obadiah 1-21|Obadiah 1}}; {{Jeremiah 49:7-22|Jeremiah 49:7–22}}).
The first return from exile took place in 538 BC. This happened after Cyrus, king of Persia, defeated Babylon ({{2 Chronicles 36:22-23|2 Chronicles 36:22–23}}; {{Ezra 1:1-4|Ezra 1:1–4}}).
This chapter is a sincere prayer asking for restoration (compare {{Daniel 9:4-19|Daniel 9:4–19}}).
There was a famine in Jerusalem during the siege, and the people ran out of food ({{2 Kings 25:3|2 Kings 25:3}}; {{Jeremiah 37:21|Jeremiah 37:21}}; {{Jeremiah 38:9|38:9}}; {{Jeremiah 52:6|52:6}}).

These terrible things happened because the people had sinned (see {{Isaiah 24:7-12|Isaiah 24:7–12}}; {{Jeremiah 7:24|Jeremiah 7:24}}; {{Jeremiah 13:18|Jeremiah 13:18}}; {{Jeremiah 25:10-11|Jeremiah 25:10–11}}; {{Amos 8:10|Amos 8:10}}).

*unless You have utterly rejected us*: The tragedy of the exile caused people to ask whether God would forgive their sin and restore them.

God answered this question through the prophets ({{Isaiah 40:27-31|Isaiah 40:27–31}}; {{Isaiah 41:8-20|41:8–20}}). He also answered it by sending Christ, who brought forgiveness and restoration ({{Matthew 9:2-6|Matthew 9:2–6}}; {{Matthew 26:28|26:28}}; {{Luke 24:47|Luke 24:47}}).
